summary: Defines managed objects for devices that implement FDDI, a fiber-optic ring network, based on the ANSI FDDI Station Management specification, so they can be monitored with SNMP. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: FDDI is a fast ring of fiber cables. This memo lists the gauges that let someone check on the ring from afar.

questions: how to manage fddi with snmp
how are fddi times converted in snmp
subtitle: SNMP-manageable objects for FDDI fiber rings, recast from the ANSI Station Management standard.

tldr.problem: Network managers needed a standard way to monitor and configure FDDI devices with SNMP, using the same definitions as the ANSI FDDI Station Management work.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module of managed objects, based on ANSI FDDI SMT 7.3, organized into SMT, MAC, Enhanced MAC Counters, PATH and PORT groups under the OBJECT IDENTIFIER fddimib.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 1285 but makes no compatibility promise with it. The RFC is now Historic.

today: RFC 1512 is Historic, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. It updates RFC 1285.

sections.title: The Network Management Framework
sections.content:
The memo sits inside the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, which has three parts: the SMI (RFC 1155, with the more concise RFC 1212) for describing and naming objects, MIB-II (RFC 1213) as the core set of managed objects, and SNMP (RFC 1157) as the protocol for network access to them.

Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and an object type plus an object instance identifies one specific instance.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a rulebook for how to name gauges, a basic set of gauges, and a way to read them over the network. This memo adds gauges for one kind of network.

sections.title: Scope and Relationship to ANSI
sections.content:
The objects apply to interfaces whose ifType is fddi(15). For these interfaces, ifSpecific in MIB-II has the value fddimib, defined as { fddi 73 }.

The definitions draw heavily on the ANSI X3T9.5 committee and its SMT subcommittee, and are identical to the ANSI ones to the maximum extent possible. The changes are syntactic only, such as remapping booleans to enumerated integers and bit strings to octet strings, so that implementations can share instrumentation with other management schemes. Only the variables that are mandatory in the ANSI specification were kept.

A few textual conventions make the module easier to read without changing encoding, for example FddiTimeNano (1 nanosecond units), FddiTimeMilli, FddiResourceId, an 8-octet FddiSMTStationIdType and a 6-octet FddiMACLongAddressType.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo copies the gauges from an existing ring-network rulebook and only rewrites them in the language that network management tools understand.

sections.title: The Object Groups
sections.content:
The module has five groups under fddimib: fddimibSMT, fddimibMAC, fddimibMACCounters, fddimibPATH and fddimibPORT. The SMT, MAC, PATH and PORT groups are mandatory for all systems that implement manageable FDDI subsystems. The Enhanced MAC Counters group is optional, but a system claiming support must implement every variable in it.

Each group starts with a count (for example fddimibSMTNumber) followed by a table of entries. The SMT table holds station-wide items such as the station ID, version IDs, connection policy and station status. Similar tables cover MAC, PATH and PORT resources, and a PATH configuration table is included. A few objects are read-write, and the rest are read-only.
sections.plainLanguage: The gauges are grouped by part of the ring: the whole station, its network card, the paths around the ring, and each plug.

sections.title: Time Values and Addresses
sections.content:
FddiTimeNano stores times in nanoseconds as a normal integer, not in the two's complement form used by ANSI. To convert an ANSI value, convert from two's complement and multiply by 80, because ANSI counts in 80 nanosecond units. The RFC's example: 8 ms is 100000 in 80 ns units, stored by ANSI as 0xFFFE7960, but reported as 8000000 over SNMP.

The station ID is 8 octets: two implementor-defined octets followed by six octets from a unique IEEE-assigned address. MAC addresses are 6 octets in the IEEE canonical notation, although addresses in FDDI SMT frames use FDDI MAC order.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook counted time in tiny odd-sized ticks. This memo says to multiply them into plain nanoseconds so any tool can read them.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1285
sections.content:
The memo updates RFC 1285. Because ANSI moved from SMT 6.2 to SMT 7.3 and the changes were so numerous, the new objects sit on a different branch of the MIB tree. The RFC says no assumptions should be made about compatibility with RFC 1285.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The new gauges were so different from the old ones that they got their own shelf, so do not assume old tools will work.

references.text: Case, J., "FDDI Management Information Base", RFC 1285, January 1992.
